title: Pawn breaks: ready or premature?
outcomes: Finds the pawn move that offers an exchange against an enemy pawn, and names the line it opens
Counts the pieces that defend and attack the break square before pushing
Says that who profits from the opened line depends on the pieces behind it
Tells a break that is supported by developed pieces from a premature one

steps.text: A **pawn break** (or lever) pushes a pawn so that it can be exchanged for an enemy pawn. It opens a file or diagonal, or changes the pawn structure. It is also how you attack a chain of pawns: strike at the **base**, the pawn at the back that protects the rest. Judge a break by what it opens and who is ready to use it.

steps.caption: Black to move. The pawn on e6 can step to e5 and attack d4.

line.say: The pawn offers an exchange. It attacks d4, and three Black pieces defend e5.
Black retakes with the bishop. The d-file and the e-file are now open.

claims.statement: After e5 the pawn attacks d4.
One White piece, the d4 pawn, attacks e5.
After the exchange the d-file and the e-file are open.
e5 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: A break is ready when pieces stand behind it. Count the defenders of the break square against the attackers, check that no pin punishes the move, and look at what the push uncovers: a pawn that leaves its square can open a diagonal or file for the opponent. In an undeveloped position a break can give the opponent targets. As a *rule of thumb*, finish development first.

steps.title: The same break, ready and premature
steps.prompt: In the first two positions Black plays ...d5 against the e4 pawn. They differ by one Black knight (on f6 or on b8). Predict each before you check. In the third, only White's e-pawn differs.

Think of the two positions where Black could play ...e5: the knight stood on c6 in one and on b8 in the other. What did you count, and what did you check besides the count, before deciding the break was ready or not? Write the numbers you looked at.
